questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spiral organisms. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the drug of choice for all stages of syphilis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the left chest and back following the dermatome. She reports severe burning pain. Which antiviral, if started within 72 hours of rash onset, reduces the risk of postherpetic neuralgia?
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg five times daily for 7 days
Valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 500 mg three times daily for 7 days
Both B and C are superior to A for reducing postherpetic neuralgia
questions.exp: Valacyclovir and famciclovir achieve higher and more sustained plasma levels than acyclovir and have been shown to more effectively reduce the duration and incidence of postherpetic neuralgia. Both are preferred over acyclovir for herpes zoster.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden facial nerve palsy and acute tenderness over the ulnar nerve. He is febrile. Which type of lepra reaction is this?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal reaction) presents with acute nerve involvement including facial nerve palsy and tender nerve trunks. It is a cell-mediated immune response seen in borderline leprosy. Treatment is prednisolone.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, malar rash, oral ulcers, arthralgia, and positive ANA (1:320, homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA antibody is highly positive. Which complement pathway abnormality is characteristically associated with her diagnosis?
opts: Low C3 and C4 with normal CH50
Low C3 and C4 with low CH50
Isolated low C3 with normal C4
questions.exp: In active SLE with nephritis, both C3 and C4 are consumed via the classical complement pathway (immune complex deposition), resulting in low C3, low C4, and low CH50. This distinguishes classical pathway activation from alternative pathway activation.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with flaccid blisters on trunk and oral erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG and C3 in intercellular spaces giving a 'fishnet' pattern. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris with mucosal involvement targets Desmoglein 3 (DSG3). Mucosal-dominant PV has antibodies only to DSG3, while mucocutaneous PV has antibodies to both DSG1 and DSG3.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with tense blisters on erythematous urticarial plaques mainly on the abdomen and thighs. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid primarily targets BP180 (BPAG2), the NC16A domain of type XVII collagen. BP230 is also targeted but BP180 antibodies correlate better with disease activity and are more pathogenic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with multiple painless red-brown papules on palms and soles, mucous patches in the mouth, and alopecia. RPR is 1:64. What is the most likely diagnosis and stage?
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis classically presents 6–8 weeks after the primary chancre with systemic features: maculopapular rash involving palms and soles (pathognomonic), mucous patches, condylomata lata, and alopecia ('moth-eaten' pattern). RPR titres are highest in this stage.

questions.q: A patient on long-term dapsone therapy develops anemia. Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies on supravital staining. What is the underlying mechanism?
opts: Megaloblastic anemia due to folate antagonism
Oxidative hemolysis due to G6PD deficiency exacerbation
Aplastic anemia due to bone marrow suppression
questions.exp: Dapsone causes oxidative hemolysis, particularly in patients with G6PD deficiency. Hydroxylamine metabolites oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin and cause denaturation producing Heinz bodies. Bite cells (degmacytes) result from splenic removal of Heinz bodies.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with erythematous, well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales over elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histology shows Munro microabscesses. Which cytokine axis is most critical in the pathogenesis?
questions.exp: Psoriasis is primarily driven by the IL-17/IL-23 (Th17) axis. IL-23 drives Th17 differentiation, which produces IL-17A causing keratinocyte proliferation and neutrophil recruitment. This is the basis for biologic therapies targeting IL-17 and IL-23.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with scaly, hypopigmented macules on the trunk. KOH preparation shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. Wood lamp shows golden-yellow fluorescence. What organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (now M. globosa is most common species). KOH shows hyphae and yeast cells resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Wood lamp shows golden-yellow or copper-orange fluorescence. Selenium sulfide or topical antifungals are used.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with multiple comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodules over the face. He has been on isotretinoin for 2 months and now develops worsening with new nodules. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.exp: Acne fulminans can be triggered by isotretinoin, especially at high starting doses. It presents with sudden severe inflammatory nodulocystic acne with systemic features (fever, arthralgia, elevated ESR). Treatment includes stopping isotretinoin and starting systemic corticosteroids.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer presents with a verrucous plaque on the foot with black dots ('sclerotic bodies'). KOH preparation shows brown muriform cells dividing in two planes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is caused by dematiaceous fungi (Fonsecaea, Cladophialophora). Pathognomonic finding is sclerotic bodies (Medlar bodies/copper pennies) — thick-walled, muriform (septated in two planes) dark brown cells on histology and KOH.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with painful cervical lymphadenopathy and a boggy, fluctuant scalp mass (kerion). KOH of hair shows ectothrix invasion. Which organism is most likely?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes kerion (inflammatory tinea capitis) with painful suppurative plaques, regional lymphadenopathy, and ectothrix (outside the hair shaft) invasion. It is a zoophilic dermatophyte. Treatment requires systemic griseofulvin or terbinafine.

questions.q: A 70-year-old immunocompromised patient develops a black necrotic eschar on the nose with periorbital swelling. CT scan shows invasion of the orbit and adjacent sinuses. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis (caused by Rhizopus arrhizus, formerly R. oryzae) presents with black necrotic eschar on the nose/palate, orbital and CNS invasion in diabetics or immunocompromised patients. Emergency treatment: liposomal amphotericin B and surgical debridement.

questions.q: A borderline tuberculoid leprosy patient has a single erythematous anesthetic plaque with raised edge. Slit-skin smear is negative. Per WHO 2018 guidelines, what treatment should be given?
opts: Rifampicin monthly + dapsone daily for 6 months
questions.exp: WHO 2018 recommends PB-MDT (paucibacillary) for 6 months for patients with 1–5 lesions and negative smear. PB-MDT consists of supervised monthly rifampicin 600 mg + dapsone 100 mg daily.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and dysphagia. ANA shows anticentromere antibody pattern. What is the most likely complication to screen for?
questions.exp: Anticentromere antibody is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST syndrome). The most serious complication is pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), which occurs in 10–15% of patients and is the leading cause of death in lcSSc. Annual echocardiography screening is recommended.

questions.q: A neonate develops a generalized exfoliative erythroderma 3 days after birth. The skin appears scalded with a positive Nikolsky sign. Blood culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. What toxin is responsible?
opts: Exfoliative toxin A and B (epidermolytic toxins)
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (serine proteases) produced by phage group II S. aureus. These toxins cleave desmoglein 1, causing intraepidermal split at the granular layer. Treatment: antistaphylococcal antibiotics (flucloxacillin).

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4: 50 cells/μL) develops multiple painless reddish-purple papules and nodules on the skin, oral mucosa, and gastrointestinal tract. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8 associated) is an AIDS-defining illness presenting with violaceous/reddish-purple lesions in multiple sites. At CD4 < 200 cells/μL, epidemic (AIDS-related) KS is common. Differentiate from bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella, responds to antibiotics) by biopsy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with photosensitive rash on the face and upper chest following a V-distribution ('shawl sign'), proximal muscle weakness, and elevated CK. Periungual erythema and Gottron's papules are present. What antibody is associated with increased risk of interstitial lung disease in this condition?
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) antibody is associated with antisynthetase syndrome: inflammatory myopathy + interstitial lung disease + mechanic's hands + Raynaud phenomenon. Anti-MDA5 is also associated with ILD (rapidly progressive). Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic dermatomyositis without ILD.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman develops a targetoid lesion with central necrosis on the palm and trunk after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Similar lesions appear on mucous membranes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) involves mucosal involvement + skin detachment < 10% BSA. The most common drugs are sulfonamides, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine), allopurinol, and NSAIDs. Target lesions with mucosal involvement and detachment < 10% = SJS; 10–30% = SJS/TEN overlap; > 30% = TEN.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a slowly growing pearly nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on the nasal tip. He is a chronic outdoor worker. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for a 0.8 cm lesion in this high-risk location?
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery is the treatment of choice for basal cell carcinoma on the nose (H-zone high-risk area) because it provides complete margin assessment while sparing maximum tissue. It has the highest cure rate for high-risk BCC locations.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a keratotic papule on the dorsum of the hand that has rapidly grown over 6 weeks into an ulcerated nodule with heaped-up edges. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Which feature indicates high-risk SCC requiring Mohs or wide excision?
questions.exp: High-risk SCC features include: size > 2 cm, depth > 4 mm or Clark level IV/V, poor differentiation, perineural/vascular invasion, immunosuppression, location on ear/lip/genitalia, and recurrence. Mohs surgery is recommended for high-risk SCC to ensure clear margins.

questions.q: During a patch test, a patient shows a ++ reaction to nickel sulfate at 48 hours. At 72-hour reading, the reaction has intensified. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes (CD4+ and CD8+). Patch testing elicits this reaction; positives at 48–72 hours that strengthen are true allergic reactions, not irritant reactions.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. What is the most appropriate treatment for a localized lesion without systemic involvement?
questions.exp: For localized impetigo (bullous or non-bullous) without systemic features, topical mupirocin 2% is the first-line treatment per Indian and international guidelines. It is effective against both S. aureus and S. pyogenes with minimal systemic absorption.

questions.q: A patient undergoing PUVA therapy for psoriasis develops a new pigmented lesion. Which long-term risk is most specifically associated with PUVA therapy?
questions.exp: Long-term PUVA therapy significantly increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), with a dose-dependent relationship. The risk is proportional to total number of PUVA sessions and cumulative UVA dose. Patients should receive periodic skin cancer surveillance.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman develops linear vesicles and blisters on sun-exposed areas of her hands and forearms after contact with wild parsnip while gardening. Which mechanism explains this reaction?
questions.exp: Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction (not immunological) caused by furocoumarins (psoralens) in plants (Umbelliferae family: parsnip, celery, lime, fig). UVA radiation activates psoralens causing DNA cross-linking, resulting in erythema, blisters, and hyperpigmentation in a streak/linear pattern.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of episodic eczematous dermatitis. IgE is markedly elevated. She has personal history of asthma and a family history of hay fever. Filaggrin gene mutations are found. Which skin barrier protein is primarily affected?
questions.exp: Filaggrin (FLG) mutations are the strongest genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis. Filaggrin is essential for skin barrier function, natural moisturizing factor production, and maintaining acidic skin pH. Mutations lead to a 'leaky' skin barrier allowing allergen penetration and sensitization.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with crops of vesicles on an erythematous base appearing in different stages (papules, vesicles, crusts). Prodromal fever and malaise preceded the rash by 2 days. What is the most common serious complication in immunocompetent children?
questions.exp: Secondary bacterial superinfection (most commonly by S. aureus and Group A Streptococcus) is the most common complication of varicella in immunocompetent children. It can present as impetigo, cellulitis, or necrotizing fasciitis. Pneumonia is more common in adults and immunocompromised.

questions.q: A patient presents for treatment of 10 warts on the soles of both feet (mosaic plantar warts). They are painful on walking. Which treatment modality uses liquid nitrogen applied with a spray gun or cotton-tipped applicator to achieve a freeze-thaw cycle?
questions.exp: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen (-196°C) is first-line treatment for warts. The freeze-thaw cycle causes intracellular ice crystal formation, cell membrane disruption, and selective destruction of infected keratinocytes. Two freeze-thaw cycles per session increase efficacy. Mosaic warts require multiple sessions.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy is being treated with MB-MDT. After 18 months of treatment, they develop fever, painful erythematous nodules on the limbs and face, and iritis. ESR is elevated. What is this reaction and its immediate treatment?
opts: Drug reaction to dapsone; stop dapsone
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) occurs in multibacillary leprosy (BL/LL), even during/after treatment. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction. Treatment: thalidomide (males, non-pregnant women) or prednisolone. MDT should be continued.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with palpable purpura over the lower legs, arthralgia, and microscopic hematuria after a streptococcal throat infection. Renal biopsy shows IgA deposits in mesangium. What is the most likely cutaneous-systemic diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) classically presents with the tetrad: palpable purpura (lower extremities/buttocks), arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal disease. IgA deposits in vessel walls and mesangium are pathognomonic. Often follows upper respiratory infection in children and adults.
